why: Trending: 'what if' science questions get huge curiosity clicks and high retention, and suit people of every age.

series.name: What If? Lab
series.style: 3D animated science film look, colourful lab, space, planets, oceans and cities, glowing holograms, bright and curious mood, vertical 9:16 frame
series.negative: text, letters, watermark, logo, gore, blood, people hurt, scary, blurry

characters.name: Dr. Nova
characters.look: Dr. Nova, a cheerful young scientist with curly purple hair, big round goggles on her forehead and a white lab coat

characters.name: Byte
characters.look: Byte, a small floating round robot with a screen face, blue glowing eyes and tiny propeller ears

rules: Each episode answers one 'What if...?' question using mainstream science, step by step, as Dr. Nova shows Byte a hologram.
Say 'scientists think' for anything uncertain. Use only well-known numbers, exactly as given in the episode idea; never invent numbers.
Exciting but never fear-mongering: no people getting hurt on screen.
Hook with the question in the first shot; end with a surprising final fact and the next question.

topics: What if the Moon disappeared? Tides would become much smaller, nights much darker, and scientists think Earth's tilt would wobble more over very long times.
What if Earth suddenly stopped spinning? Everything not fixed down would keep moving east at the speed of Earth's spin, which is about 1,670 km/h at the equator, and a day would last a whole year.
What if you fell into a black hole? The pull on your feet would be much stronger than on your head, stretching you like spaghetti (spaghettification).
What if all the ice on Earth melted? Scientists estimate sea levels would rise by about 70 metres, changing every coastline.
What if all the bees disappeared? About one third of the food crops we eat depend on pollinators like bees.
What if the Sun switched off? We would not notice for about 8 minutes, the time sunlight takes to reach Earth.
What if you could dig a tunnel straight through the Earth? You would pass through the hot mantle and the iron core, hotter than the surface of the Sun.
What if we lived on Mars? Gravity there is about 38% of Earth's, so you could jump almost three times higher, but the air is too thin to breathe.
What if you never drank water? Most people can only survive about three days without water.
What if gravity were twice as strong? Everything would feel twice as heavy, and walking up stairs would be like carrying another person.
What if the internet went down worldwide for one day? Payments, messages, maps and many businesses would stop.
What if dinosaurs never went extinct? Scientists think mammals, and maybe humans, might never have become dominant.
What if Earth were flat? It could not happen: gravity pulls a planet-sized mass into a ball.
What if there were no friction? You could not walk, hold a cup or tie your shoes; everything would slide forever.
What if mosquitoes vanished? Fewer diseases like malaria, but some fish and birds that eat them would lose food.
moreIdeas: What if humans could make food from sunlight like plants? We would need skin as big as a tennis court and would still need to eat.
What if you didn't sleep for a week? Memory, mood and reaction time get much worse; sleep is when the brain sorts memories.
What if there was twice as much oxygen in the air? Fires would burn much more easily; long ago, high oxygen levels let insects grow giant.
What if Earth had rings like Saturn? They would stretch across the sky as a giant bright arch, visible even in the day.
What if humans had tails? Our ancestors did long ago; we still have a tailbone (coccyx).
What if you could see heat like a snake? Some snakes have pits that sense infrared, so warm animals glow in the dark.
What if Earth were twice as big? Gravity would be stronger, the air thicker, and rockets would struggle to reach space.
What if a day lasted 48 hours? Days and nights would be much hotter and colder, and our body clocks would be confused.
What if we could talk to animals? We would learn how bees dance to share directions and how elephants call over long distances.
What if lightning struck the sea near you? The electricity spreads out across the surface, so being far away and in a safe place matters.
